identity.title: Pluto's atmosphere observations with ALMA: Spatially-resolved maps of CO and HCN emission and first detection of HNC

paper_type_evidence.quote: We report on new observations of Pluto’s atmosphere with ALMA, performed in April and July/August 2017 with two main goals: (i) obtaining spatially-resolved measurements ($\sim$0.06” on the $\sim$0.15” disk subtended by Pluto and its atmosphere) of CO(3-2) and HCN(4-3) (ii) targetting new chemical compounds, primarily hydrogen isocyanide (HNC) .
We obtained a new set of observations of the Pluto-Charon system with the 12-m array of the Large Millimeter Array (ALMA), under the ALMA project 2016.1.00426.S.

question.value: Obtain spatially-resolved measurements of CO(3-2) and HCN(4-3) in Pluto's atmosphere to investigate vertical and horizontal variations in temperature and composition, and search for new atmospheric compounds, primarily hydrogen isocyanide (HNC).

evidence.quote: We report on new observations of Pluto’s atmosphere with ALMA, performed in April and July/August 2017 with two main goals: (i) obtaining spatially-resolved measurements ($\sim$0.06” on the $\sim$0.15” disk subtended by Pluto and its atmosphere) of CO(3-2) and HCN(4-3) (ii) targetting new chemical compounds, primarily hydrogen isocyanide (HNC) .

A specific advantage is that currently Pluto’s North pole is well positioned for viewing from Earth (sub-Earth latitude on Pluto $\sim$ 50-57$^\circ$ N over 2015-2020) enabling the investigation of equatorial-to-pole variations in the temperature and composition fields.
We obtained a new set of observations of the Pluto-Charon system with the 12-m array of the Large Millimeter Array (ALMA), under the ALMA project 2016.1.00426.S.
This paper is based on ALMA program 2016.1.00426.S.

analysis_steps.goal: Extract zero-spacing (total flux density) CO and HCN spectra via visibility fitting and generate image cubes

method.value: Fit spectral line visibilities per channel over u-v range <= 1000 klambda (excluding Charon, forcing Pluto at phase center) to derive zero-spacing spectra for individual dates and combined data. Produce image cubes for combined CO/HCN data and HNC setup.

evidence.quote: For the CO/HCN setup observations, we next fitted the visibilities in the spectral line windows on a per-channel basis, in order to determine the best value of the total flux density (a.k.a. zero spacing flux) as a function of channel.
For this fitting, we excluded the Charon contribution and fitted the visibilities over a maximum u-v range of 1000 k$\lambda$, forcing Pluto to be at phase center.
Finally we produced image cubes for all of the spectral windows, for the combined CO/HCN data, and the HNC observation.

method.value: Integrate CO over +/-5 MHz and HCN over +/-1 MHz from line center, and take continuum over +/-10-40 MHz. Average spectra in oversampled radial bins of 0.007" globally and split into four azimuthal quadrants (low vs high latitudes, morning vs evening). Estimate uncertainties via Monte Carlo noise clones.

evidence.quote: The CO and HCN emissions, expressed in mJy$\cdot$MHz/beam, are integrated over $\pm$5 MHz and $\pm$1 MHz, respectively, from line center, and the continuum (in mJy/beam) is taken in the immediate vicinity of the lines ($\pm$10-40 MHz from line center).
To visualize these effects in more details, we averaged spectra in (oversampled) bins of 0.007" in radial distance, and calculated the CO and HCN line areas for each bin.

evidence.quote: To estimate error bars on these areas, we generated, for each bin, a series of “clones" of the observed spectrum, adding random spectral noise at the relevant level, and calculating the line area for each of these clones; the rms dispersion in the resulting areas yielded the desired error bar.

analysis_steps.goal: Retrieve disk-averaged and spatially-resolved temperature profiles and CO mixing ratios

method.value: Use a 200-layer (0-1450 km) spherical non-scattering radiative transfer code convolved with the synthesized beam, coupled with a constrained and regularized Conrath/Rodgers inversion algorithm over +/-30 MHz from CO line core. First invert 2017 zero-spacing and 2015 disk-center CO spectra, then invert 2017 spatially-resolved spectra on a 21x21 grid (0.1" x 0.1" with 0.01" sampling) under 4 CO/temperature scenarios, and construct zonal mean temperature fields.

evidence.quote: The model, presented in Paper I (where all model details can be found), was extended to cover the 0-1450 km altitude range by means of 200 layers, with an altitude-varying layer thickness.
The inversion scheme was applied to the measured fluxes (in Jy or Jy/beam) over $\pm$30 MHz from the CO line core (i.e. 345.766–345.826 GHz).
To ensure comfortable beam oversampling, CO spectra were inverted over a grid of 0.1” x 0.1” with 0.01” sampling (i.e. 21 x 21 spectra to invert).

key_parameters.value: 200 atmospheric layers from 0 to 1450 km; fitting interval = +/-30 MHz (345.766-345.826 GHz); maximum 2 iterations (1 iteration if rms decreases by < 2%)

evidence.quote: The model, presented in Paper I (where all model details can be found), was extended to cover the 0-1450 km altitude range by means of 200 layers, with an altitude-varying layer thickness.
The inversion scheme was applied to the measured fluxes (in Jy or Jy/beam) over $\pm$30 MHz from the CO line core (i.e. 345.766–345.826 GHz).

the inversion process was limited to a maximum of two iterations, and even only one if the rms between the model and the data, calculated over the fitting interval, had decreased by less than 2 % after the first iteration.

In all cases, a 600 ppm CO mixing ratio and the disk-integrated temperature profile retrieved previously were used as a priori.

evidence.loc: Initial fitting attempts of the emission radial profiles
evidence.quote: A CO mixing ratio of 515 ppm (Paper I) and a brightness surface temperature of 33.0 K were used.
The method involves the initialization of the CO mixing ratio (assumed constant with altitude) and the temperature profile to initial (“a priori”) values.

fitting.value: Constrained and regularized iterative inversion (Conrath et al., 1998; Rodgers, 2000) evaluated with chi^2 over +/-30 MHz and reduced chi^2 (S) over +/-10 MHz

evidence.quote: Following the approach of Paper I, we analyzed the CO data using a constrained and regularized inversion method based on algorithms detailed in (cite: conrath98) and (cite: rodgers00).

The fitting quality of the a priori and of the solution were quantified by $\chi^2$ statistics, both in unreduced form ($\chi^2$ = $\Sigma$ \[(model$_i$-obs$_i$)/$\sigma_i$\] $^2$ where $i$ refers to the $N$ independent frequencies in the $\pm$30 MHz fitting interval) and in reduced form $S$ = $\sqrt{\chi'^2/N'}$ (in this case, $\chi'^2$ was calculated over the $N'$ frequencies within $\pm$10 MHz

validation.value: Tested 4 inversion variants (fixed CO=600 ppm; fixed T; free CO and T; fixed spatially-variable CO=800-4*lambda ppm), two zonal-mean averaging methods, and an alternate 3-unit physical surface temperature model (Lellouch et al., 2016)

evidence.quote: The variants, shown from left to right in Fig. 6, include the following cases: (1) fixed, uniform, CO = 600 ppm, free thermal profile (2) fixed thermal profile, free CO (3) free CO and thermal profiles (4) fixed, but spatially variable CO, free thermal profiles.

This process however led to atmospheric temperature fields that were not significantly different from those inferred with a constant surface temperature model, leading us to believe our result is also robust in this respect.

analysis_steps.goal: Determine the mean vertical profile of HCN and search for spatial variations in HCN

method.value: Run a parametric forward-model grid varying lower-atmosphere scaling f_low, top altitude z_top, top mixing ratio q_top, and shape exponent alpha. Fit to 2017 radial HCN line areas (9 bins of 0.014"), 2017 zero-spacing line, and 2015 disk-center line. Then invert spatially-resolved HCN spectra at each beam position (0.01" grid) by fitting a constant scaling factor to the nominal 2017 HCN profile (and alternatively test upper-atmosphere temperature inversions).

evidence.quote: We ran a grid of models varying f$_{low}$, z$_{top}$, q$_{top}$, and $\alpha$. f$_{low}$ values of 0.01, 0.1, 0.5, 1, 1.5 and 2 were tested
Models were compared to data averaged in 9 bins of radial distance, with a bin size of 0.014", i.e. bins at \[0-0.014"\], \[0.014-0.028"\],...,\[0.112-0.126"\].
In a second step, we inverted the HCN line profiles at each beam position to search for possible spatial variations of the HCN abundance.
where q$_{min}$ is the HCN mixing ratio at z$_{min}$ = 230 km in the (possibly rescaled by f$_{low}$) (cite: lavvas21) profile
We ran a grid of models varying f$_{low}$, z$_{top}$, q$_{top}$, and $\alpha$. f$_{low}$ values of 0.01, 0.1, 0.5, 1, 1.5 and 2 were tested
For the $\alpha$ exponent, we used $\alpha$ = 1.4, 2, 3, 4.5 and 6, which adequately samples a variety of profile shapes. We explored z$_{top}$ in the range 400-1300 km by steps of 50 km.

assumptions.value: Single 2017 disk-averaged retrieved thermal profile holds at all beam positions (relaxing to New Horizons profile above 400 km)

evidence.quote: For this task, we used the retrieved disk-averaged thermal profile for 2017 for all beam positions.
Information on the upper atmosphere thermal structure is thus best provided by the New Horizons profile (cite: young18), towards which our CO-derived profiles relax above 400 km.

fitting.value: Grid search minimizing chi^2; acceptable fits defined by S_areas,2017 = sqrt(chi^2_areas,2017 / 9) < 1.0 and S_line,2015 = sqrt(chi^2_line,2015 / N_o) < 1.2 over +/-4 MHz

evidence.quote: Acceptable fits were defined as those which satisfied a mean deviation, rescaled to the measurement error bar, lower than 1.0 per point in the observable, i.e. S$_{areas,2017}$ = $\sqrt{\chi^2_{areas,2017}/9}$ $<$ 1.0.
the integral runs over the N$_o$ spectra points within $\pm$ 4 MHz from line center; acceptable fits for 2015 were defined by S$_{line,2015}$ = $\sqrt{\chi^2_{line,2015}/N_o}$ $<$ 1.2.

validation.value: Joint comparison of 2017 radial line areas, 2017 total flux spectrum, and 2015 disk-averaged spectrum; tested alternative hypothesis of upper-atmosphere temperature variations

evidence.quote: The same parameterized profiles were used to calculate the HCN total (zero-spacing) line in 2017, and the disk-center line in the conditions of the 2015 observation.
We explored another avenue, namely that the spatial variability of the HCN fluxes could be related to temperature variations in the upper atmospheric region ($>$ 600 km) probed by the HCN emission.

analysis_steps.goal: Derive HNC column density and upper limits on H13CN, HC15N, HC3N, CH3CN, and CH3CCH

findings_qualitative.value: Spatially-resolved CO(3-2) spectra exhibit an absorption core at beam positions within Pluto's disk that vanishes towards the limb, providing direct spectral evidence of Pluto's cold mesosphere (negative temperature gradient above ~30 km).

evidence.quote: The CO line shows an absorption core at beam positions within Pluto’s disk, a direct signature of Pluto’s cold mesosphere.
A new observational result to highlight is the presence of absorption cores for many beam positions, most prominent near disk center and progressively vanishing towards Pluto’s limb.

findings_qualitative.value: HCN(4-3) emission is much more spatially extended than CO(3-2) and continuum emission, peaking slightly beyond Pluto's limb (~0.065" or ~1.3 Pluto radii).

evidence.quote: On the other hand, the radial distribution of the HCN emission is markedly different, peaking slightly beyond Pluto’s limb.

evidence.loc: Initial fitting attempts of the emission radial profiles
evidence.quote: in the observations, the HCN emission does not decrease before $\sim$0.065” from disk center, i.e. at $\sim$1.3 Pluto radius.

findings_qualitative.value: HCN emission is enhanced above the low-latitude (sky North-East) limb compared to the high-latitude (sky South-West) limb, opposite to the CO emission trend.

evidence.quote: Fig. 2 further shows that the CO emission appears to be enhanced at high Northern latitudes compared to Equatorial latitudes, and the opposite is generally seen for HCN.
In spite of these difficulties, our observations indicate larger HCN amounts, by a factor of several, above Pluto’s low-latitude vs high-latitude limb.

findings_qualitative.value: Low HCN abundance in the lower atmosphere and low upper limits on CH3CN and CH3CCH indicate incomplete resublimation of ice-coated haze aerosols in the lower atmosphere.

evidence.quote: These upper limits also point to incomplete resublimation of ice-coated aerosols in the lower atmosphere.

Our new upper limit (5$\times$10$^{-9}$ at 65 km) is $\sim$5 times smaller than the saturated value at 100 K (and $\sim$50 times smaller than saturation at 107 K), implying that resublimation is not complete, and lower than modeled by (cite: lavvas21).

claims.hypothesis: Pluto's lower atmosphere (near the 30 km stratopause) exhibits latitudinal temperature variations between the summer North Pole and low latitudes.
claims.experiment: Spatially-resolved ALMA mapping of CO(3-2) at ~0.06" resolution and regularized radiative transfer inversions across a 21x21 spatial grid under multiple CO distribution and surface temperature assumptions.
claims.result: Enhanced CO line emission at high Northern latitudes (at the 2-sigma level over 0.03-0.07") is best explained by summer pole temperatures near 30 km being 7 +/- 3.5 K warmer than low latitudes.
claims.finding: Tentative evidence for a warmer summer pole stratopause (by 7 +/- 3.5 K), which may point to shorter radiative timescales in Pluto's atmosphere than predicted by gas-only models, possibly due to radiative control by haze.

evidence.quote: Analysis of the CO line map provides tentative evidence for a non-uniform temperature field in the lower atmosphere (near 30 km), with summer pole latitudes being 7$\pm$3.5 K warmer than low latitudes. This unexpected result may point to shorter radiative timescales in the atmosphere than previously thought.
In summary our preferred interpretation of the larger CO line areas at high vs low latitudes is that they result from enhanced near-stratopause temperatures, by 7$\pm$3.5 K.

claims.hypothesis: The radial distribution of spatially-resolved HCN(4-3) emission constrains the vertical profile of HCN in Pluto's atmosphere.
claims.experiment: Parametric forward modeling of HCN vertical profiles compared against the 2017 radial variation of HCN line areas (9 radial bins), the 2017 total flux spectrum, and the 2015 disk-averaged spectrum.
claims.result: HCN emission peaks beyond the limb (~1.3 Pluto radii), yielding a column-averaged HCN altitude of 690 +/- 75 km, an upper-atmosphere (>800 km) mixing ratio of ~1.8e-4, and a lower-atmosphere (65 km) mixing ratio < 5e-9.
claims.finding: HCN is predominantly located in the upper atmosphere (mean altitude 690 +/- 75 km) where it is highly supersaturated, while little or no HCN is present in the lower atmosphere (< 5e-9 at 65 km), implying undersaturation and incomplete resublimation of ice-coated aerosols there.

evidence.quote: The mean (column-averaged) location of HCN is at 690$\pm$75 km altitude, with an upper atmosphere ($>$800 km) mixing ratio of $\sim$1.8$\times$10$^{-4}$. Little or no HCN ($<$5$\times$10$^{-9}$ at 65 km) is present in the lower atmosphere, implying undersaturation of HCN there.

claims.hypothesis: Hydrogen isocyanide (HNC) is present and detectable in Pluto's atmosphere at levels comparable to Titan's atmosphere.
claims.experiment: Disk-averaged ALMA observations of HNC(3-2) at 271.981 GHz in configuration C40.3 and radiative transfer modeling using uniform cutoff models and rescaled photochemical/observational templates.
claims.result: HNC(3-2) is detected with a peak S/N of 4.0 and line area of 6.75 +/- 1.70 mJy MHz, corresponding to a surface-referred column density of (7.0 +/- 2.1)e12 cm^-2 and an HNC/HCN ratio of 0.095 +/- 0.026.
claims.finding: First detection of HNC in Pluto's atmosphere (second planetary atmosphere after Titan), with a column density and HNC/HCN ratio very similar to Titan's, requiring inclusion of the HNCH+ + HNC -> HCN + HCNH+ isomerisation reaction in photochemical models.

evidence.quote: The first detection of HNC is reported, with a (7.0$\pm$2.1)$\times$10$^{12}$ cm$^{-2}$ column density, referred to Pluto surface, and a HNC / HCN ratio of 0.095$\pm$0.026, very similar to their values in Titan’s atmosphere.

evidence.loc: HNC detection and upper limits on other compounds: comparison to photochemical models
evidence.quote: Including it back in the reaction scheme does decrease (resp. increase) the HNC (resp. HCN) abundance. The resulting HNC column density, 1.4$\times$10$^{13}$ cm$^{-2}$, is still overpredicted by a factor $\sim$2, but the HNC/HCN ratio becomes 0.11, now consistent with the measured range.

claims.hypothesis: CH3CCH is present in Pluto's atmosphere at the column density of 2.5e15 cm^-2 (vertical) reported from New Horizons Alice UV observations by Steffl et al. (2020).
claims.experiment: Search for the CH3CCH J = 14 multiplet around 256.258 GHz in the ALMA HNC setup data and radiative transfer modeling using rescaled Lavvas et al. (2021) profiles.
claims.result: CH3CCH is not detected, placing an upper limit on the vertical column density of < 8.5e14 cm^-2 (3 times smaller than the New Horizons Alice value).
claims.finding: The ALMA upper limit on CH3CCH is inconsistent with the reported New Horizons detection by Steffl et al. (2020), casting doubt on that identification and supporting reduced resublimation of ice-coated aerosols in the lower atmosphere.

evidence.quote: We also obtain upper limits on CH$_3$CN ($<$2.6$\times$10$^{13}$ cm$^{-2}$) and CH$_3$CCH ($<$8.5$\times$10$^{14}$ cm$^{-2}$); the latter value is inconsistent with the reported detection of CH$_3$CCH from New Horizons.

why_this_data.value: Intermediate ALMA configurations (C40.7, ~0.06" resolution) resolve Pluto's disk (~0.10") and extended atmosphere (~0.15") while retaining sufficient sensitivity for weak atmospheric lines (60-100 mJy), and Pluto's high sub-Earth latitude (~53.5 deg N) allows probing equator-to-pole variations; compact configuration C40.3 (~0.58") maximizes sensitivity for detecting faint HNC while separating Pluto from Charon.

evidence.quote: However, intermediate array configurations of several 10’s of milli-arcseconds (mas) do allow resolution of Pluto’s atmosphere, while providing sufficient sensitivity. A specific advantage is that currently Pluto’s North pole is well positioned for viewing from Earth (sub-Earth latitude on Pluto $\sim$ 50-57$^\circ$ N over 2015-2020) enabling the investigation of equatorial-to-pole variations in the temperature and composition fields.

Because the prime goal of the HNC setup observations was detection, we used a low spatial resolution (ALMA configuration C40.3, with maximum baseline $\sim$460 m and resolution $\sim$0.58$\mbox{$^{\prime\prime}$}$), sufficient to separate Pluto from Charon, while ensuring the entire flux density from Pluto would be measured.

why_this_method.value: A constrained and regularized Conrath/Rodgers inversion method is used for CO to retrieve vertical temperature profiles without unphysical oscillations, whereas a parametric forward-modeling grid and single-parameter scaling are used for HCN because the narrow, minimally pressure-broadened HCN lines lack sufficient vertical information content (~1.5 independent layers) and hyperfine satellite lines are not clearly detected in the resolved 2017 data.

evidence.quote: temperature profiles are (i) constrained to remain close to the a priori at levels where the measurements contain no information (ii) regularized, i.e. smoothed to some vertical resolution (usually comparable to the atmospheric scale height) to avoid unphysical oscillations of the solution profiles.

When fitting the spectra at each beam position, we allowed for a single free parameter, namely a constant scaling factor to this profile. The reason for this decision is the limited information content of the HCN narrow (minimally pressure-broadened) spectra, preventing us from retrieving a HCN vertical profile from lineshape.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Atmospheric decorrelation correction using check source J1923-2104 (not needed because continuum flux density was sufficient for self-calibration)

evidence.quote: An additional source, J1923-2104, was included as a “check source”. ALMA includes these sources to allow for an atmospheric decorrelation correction, if needed. However, as described below, there was enough flux density to self-calibrate the data so this correction was not necessary.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Explaining high-latitude CO emission enhancement solely via a latitudinal CO abundance increase toward the North Pole with fixed temperature (disfavored because it yields the smallest chi^2 improvement and contradicts GCM predictions of a North-to-South sublimation flow that transports CO to the southern hemisphere)

evidence.quote: The free CO, fixed temperature, retrievals (second column) would point to somewhat more marked CO variations, but we note that it is the one associated with the smallest “gain" in $\chi^2$ (last line in Fig.6). Furthermore, a CO increase from the Equator to the North Pole is not expected.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Explaining enhanced low-latitude HCN emission via a ~400 km thick 'hot layer' peaking at 90 K at 800 km altitude (discarded because it is grossly inconsistent with 65-68 K temperatures inferred from New Horizons Alice/REX CH4 profiles, requires ~5 times more thermal conduction than solar EUV/FUV heating can sustain, and produces discrepant profiles at the polar limb)

evidence.quote: However, the thermal profiles returned at these beam positions were found to exhibit a broad ($\sim$400 km FWHM) “hot layer", with peak temperatures of 90 K at 800 km. This i.e. $\sim$20 K higher than the “canonical" 70 K upper atmosphere temperature, and as discussed below grossly inconsistent with inferences from New Horizons / Alice at low latitudes.
We therefore did not consider this solution any further.

limitations_admitted.value: The retrieved latitudinal temperature contrast (7 +/- 3.5 K) is only ~2-sigma significant, improvement over the a priori fit (Delta chi^2) is modest, and temperatures retrieved near the polar limb 'beyond' the pole are somewhat higher than near disk center at the same latitudes.

evidence.quote: Within these error bars, the temperature latitude variations are only $\sim$2-$\sigma$ significant

While our analysis hints at an elevated stratopause temperature above the summer pole, the comparison of the first two panels of Fig. 8, the maps of $\Delta\chi^2$ (fifth panel of Fig. 6), and visual inspection of Fig. 7, admittedly invites to caution.

Another note of concern may be the fact that atmospheric temperatures at Northern latitudes (50$^\circ$N-70$^\circ$N) are returned to be somewhat higher from the near-limb position “beyond" the pole than from the near disk-center beam position

limitations_admitted.value: The 2015 disk-averaged and 2017 disk-resolved datasets do not provide fully consistent results on the HCN vertical distribution, especially if a large lower-atmosphere HCN component is included.

evidence.quote: A general result is that while the increase with altitude of HCN, inferred from the 2015 spectrum shape, is confirmed from the HCN emission radial distribution in the 2017 data, the two datasets do not appear to provide fully consistent results on the HCN vertical distribution.

limitations_admitted.value: Models of spatial variations in HCN underpredict the observed HCN line areas and contrasts at/beyond the low-latitude limb (reduced chi^2 up to ~1.4), and a satisfactory physical explanation for enhanced low-latitude HCN is lacking.

evidence.quote: in fact the HCN line areas and contrasts at/beyond the low-latitude (sky North-East) limbs are somewhat underpredicted by the model (this can be seen e.g. in Fig. 10, at beam positions near (RA, DEC) = (0.04", 0.04"), and the reduced $\chi^2$ between modelled and observed spectra reaches values of $\sim$1.4

In summary, we suggest that the spatial variations of the HCN emission point to enhanced HCN abundances at low vs high latitudes, perhaps combined with some temperature variations in the upper atmosphere, but recognize we are at loss to propose a satisfactory explanation for them.

referee_caveats_inferred: The spatial resolution (~0.076" x 0.052") only marginally resolves Pluto's ~0.10" solid disk (fewer than ~2-3 independent beams across the disk), so beam smearing strongly couples disk and limb emission.
Combining three CO/HCN epochs with different sub-Earth longitudes (165-162 deg, 253-249 deg, 85-82 deg) smears out any longitudinal or local-time surface/atmosphere heterogeneity.

reproducibility.estimated_data_volume_inferred: Moderate (~20-50 GB of raw ALMA visibilities for 4 execution blocks in Band 6 and Band 7)
reproducibility.score_reason: Observational setups, flux-scale anchoring (33 K), visibility fitting parameters, and retrieval equations/grids are thoroughly documented, and the ALMA data (2016.1.00426.S) are public in the archive. However, the custom radiative transfer and inversion code is not publicly available, and low-level AIPS/GILDAS imaging parameters are omitted.
reproducibility.rediscovery_reason: The raw ALMA data for 2016.1.00426.S are public, the flux calibration anchoring to Pluto's 33 K continuum is explicitly given, and the main observational results (first detection and integrated line flux/column density of HNC, radial extension of HCN vs CO, absorption cores in resolved CO spectra, and upper limits on CH3CN/CH3CCH) are numeric and can be independently reproduced from the visibility data.
